weathering-vs-erosion.ncertRef: NCERT Class 7 Geography, Chapter 3 — Our Changing Earth; extended in Class 9 and Class 11 Physical Geography.

explainers.term: What weathering actually means
paras: Weathering is the breaking down of rocks, soil and minerals where they already sit. The Latin root is the giveaway: it is the weather — rain, frost, heat, wind, dissolved gases — working on a rock face over years. Nothing is carried away. A boulder that cracks into six pieces but stays on the same hillside has been weathered, not eroded.

Because nothing moves, weathering is described as an in-situ (in place) process. It is the first stage in the long chain that turns solid bedrock into loose sediment and eventually into soil. Without weathering there would be no loose material for any other process to pick up, which is why every textbook treats it as the starting point.

explainers.term: What erosion actually means
paras: Erosion is the removal and carrying away of that loosened material to somewhere else. It needs a transporting agent — running water, wind, moving ice or sea waves — and it always involves a change of place. The river that lifts weathered sand from a hillside and drops it 200 km downstream has eroded it.

Erosion is usually followed by transportation (the journey) and deposition (the drop-off). A delta at a river's mouth is made entirely of material that was weathered upstream, eroded, transported and finally deposited.

sections.h: The three types of weathering
paras: CBSE asks for these by name, so learn the type and one example of each.
bullets: Physical (mechanical) weathering — rock breaks apart without any change in its chemical make-up. Water seeps into a crack, freezes overnight, expands by about 9% and levers the crack wider; repeat this for a few winters and the rock splits. This is called frost wedging. In hot deserts, daily heating and night-time cooling makes the outer layer peel off in sheets — exfoliation.

Chemical weathering — the minerals themselves change into new substances. Rainwater dissolves carbon dioxide from the air to make weak carbonic acid, which slowly dissolves limestone; this is carbonation, and it is how limestone caves and the karst landscape of Meghalaya formed. Iron-bearing rocks turn reddish-brown as they react with oxygen and moisture — oxidation, the same chemistry as rust.

Biological weathering — living things do the work. Tree roots widen cracks as they thicken, lichens release acids that eat into rock surfaces, and burrowing animals expose fresh rock to air and water.

sections.h: The four agents of erosion and the landforms they leave
paras: Each agent leaves a signature set of landforms. Examiners frequently give you the landform and ask for the agent, so learn them as pairs.
bullets: Running water (rivers) — the most powerful agent overall. Erosional landforms: V-shaped valleys, gorges, waterfalls, meanders. Depositional landforms: floodplains, ox-bow lakes, levees and deltas. The Sundarbans delta is the classic Indian example.

Wind — dominant in deserts where there is no vegetation to hold the surface. It carves mushroom rocks (the base is worn faster because most sand is carried near the ground) and builds sand dunes and loess deposits.
Glaciers (moving ice) — grind out U-shaped valleys, cirques and hanging valleys, and dump unsorted debris as moraines. Seen across the Himalayas.
Sea waves — cut sea caves, which widen into sea arches, which collapse to leave sea stacks and steep sea cliffs.

sections.h: How the two fit together
paras: Weathering and erosion are sequential, not competing. The standard chain is: weathering breaks the rock → erosion picks the pieces up → transportation carries them → deposition drops them. Geographers group weathering, erosion and transportation together under one umbrella term, denudation, meaning the overall stripping-away of the land surface.

The practical consequence is that weathering can happen entirely on its own, but erosion cannot get started without material that has already been loosened. That asymmetry is the single most examined idea in this topic.

examples.t: A cracked rock on a Himalayan slope
examples.d: Water froze in the crack each night and split the rock. The pieces are still lying where they fell. Weathering only — no transport has happened.

examples.t: The Ganga carrying brown silt
examples.d: That silt was weathered off rocks upstream and is now being transported. This is erosion in progress; it will end as deposition in the Sundarbans delta.

examples.t: A rusty-red rock face in the Deccan
examples.d: Iron minerals have reacted with oxygen and moisture. Chemical weathering — the rock's composition itself has changed.

examples.t: A mushroom rock in the Thar Desert
examples.d: Wind-blown sand wore the base away faster than the top. Wind erosion, because the worn-off sand has been carried elsewhere.

mistakes: Writing that weathering 'moves' rock. It never does — the moment material is carried away, the process is erosion.
Treating erosion as the opposite of weathering. They are consecutive stages of one chain, not opposites.
Saying erosion causes weathering. It is the other way round: weathering supplies the loose material that erosion then removes.
Confusing erosion with deposition. Erosion is the picking-up and carrying; deposition is the dropping-off at the end of the journey.
Forgetting biological weathering. Many students list only physical and chemical and lose a mark.

quiz.q: A rock on a hillside splits into pieces after repeated freezing and thawing, but all the pieces remain in place. This is:
quiz.why: The rock broke down where it stood and nothing was carried away, which is the definition of weathering.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an agent of erosion?
quiz.why: Temperature change breaks rock in place, so it is an agent of physical weathering. Erosion needs an agent that transports material.

quiz.q: Limestone caves are formed mainly by:
quiz.why: Rainwater with dissolved carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone — carbonation, a chemical process.

quiz.q: The correct order of the denudation chain is:
quiz.why: Rock must first be broken down in place before any agent can remove, carry and finally drop it.

extraFaqs.q: Which happens first, weathering or erosion?
extraFaqs.a: Weathering happens first. It breaks the rock into loose fragments where they stand; only then can an agent such as water or wind pick those fragments up and carry them away, which is erosion.

extraFaqs.q: Is soil formation weathering or erosion?
extraFaqs.a: Soil formation begins with weathering. Rock is broken down in place into fine mineral particles, which then mix with decayed organic matter (humus) to become soil. Erosion actually removes topsoil, so it works against soil formation.

extraFaqs.q: Can erosion happen without weathering?
extraFaqs.a: Essentially no. Erosion needs loose material to carry, and weathering is what produces that loose material. The only partial exception is where an agent is powerful enough to pluck at solid rock directly, such as a fast river or a glacier, but even there weathering has usually weakened the rock first.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between erosion and deposition?
extraFaqs.a: Erosion is the removal and carrying away of material. Deposition is the dropping of that material when the transporting agent loses energy — a river slowing at its mouth, or wind dropping sand to build a dune.

explainers.term: What a physical map shows
paras: A physical map — also called a relief map — shows the natural features of the Earth's surface. Mountains, plateaus, plains, deserts, rivers, lakes and oceans all appear, and none of it depends on human decisions. If every border in the world were redrawn tomorrow, a physical map of India would look exactly the same.

Physical maps use a colour convention you are expected to know: green for plains and lowlands, yellow and brown for higher ground with darker browns for the highest mountains, blue for water bodies, and white for snow-covered peaks. That colouring is what lets you read height from a flat sheet of paper.

explainers.term: What a political map shows
paras: A political map shows features created by people and agreed by governments: country boundaries, state and district borders, capitals and major cities. Everything on it is a human decision, which means a political map can go out of date. India's political map changed when Telangana was formed in 2014 and again when Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh became separate Union Territories in 2019.

Political maps use a different convention: each state or country gets its own flat colour so neighbours are easy to tell apart, boundaries are drawn as distinct lines, and capitals are usually marked with a star or a circled dot.

sections.h: The three things every map must have
paras: Whatever its type, the NCERT syllabus says a map has three components. Questions on this come up almost every year.
bullets: Distance (scale) — the ratio between a distance on the map and the real distance on the ground. A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map equals 50,000 cm, or half a kilometre, in reality.
Direction — shown by a north line or a compass rose. The four cardinal directions are north, south, east and west; north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west are the intermediate directions.
Symbols — standard signs and colours that let a small sheet carry a lot of information. Because symbols are internationally agreed, a map is readable even by someone who cannot read its language.

sections.h: The third type: thematic maps
paras: Students often assume there are only two kinds of map, and lose marks for it. A thematic map shows one specific theme or piece of information — rainfall distribution, population density, road and rail networks, crop patterns, or forest cover.

Thematic maps are the ones you meet most often outside the classroom: a weather map on the news, a metro route map, an election results map. They may be drawn on top of either a physical or a political base.

sections.h: Map versus plan, and what scale changes
paras: A closely related distinction is between a map and a plan. A plan is a drawing of a very small area — a house, a school building, a plot of land — drawn to a large scale so that fine detail is visible. A map covers a much larger area at a smaller scale.

Scale is what makes this work. A large-scale map covers a small area with a lot of detail; a small-scale map covers a large area with little detail. A map of your town is large scale; a map of the whole world is small scale. The wording feels backwards to most students, which is exactly why it is examined.

examples.t: Finding the Western Ghats
examples.d: Use a physical map. Mountain ranges are natural features, shown in brown shading.

examples.t: Finding the capital of Rajasthan
examples.d: Use a political map. Capitals are human-designated and marked with a star.

examples.t: Finding where the monsoon brings most rain
examples.d: Use a thematic map — specifically a rainfall distribution map.

examples.t: Finding the route of the Godavari
examples.d: Use a physical map. Rivers are natural features, drawn in blue.

mistakes: Saying a physical map shows 'no cities at all'. Many physical maps do mark major cities for reference; the point is that its main purpose is natural features.
Forgetting thematic maps exist as a third category.
Mixing up large scale and small scale. Large scale = small area, more detail.
Writing that a political map never changes. It changes whenever boundaries are redrawn.
Confusing a plan with a map — a plan covers a very small area at a large scale.

quiz.q: Which map would you use to locate the Deccan Plateau?
quiz.why: A plateau is a natural landform, so it appears on a physical (relief) map.

quiz.q: On a physical map, brown usually represents:
quiz.why: The standard convention is green for plains, brown and yellow for higher ground, blue for water and white for snow.

quiz.q: A map showing the distribution of rainfall across India is a:
quiz.why: A map devoted to one specific theme, such as rainfall, is a thematic map.

quiz.q: A scale of 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map equals:
quiz.why: 1 cm represents 50,000 cm on the ground. 50,000 cm = 500 m = half a kilometre.

extraFaqs.q: What are the three types of maps?
extraFaqs.a: Physical maps show natural features such as mountains, plateaus, plains and rivers. Political maps show human-made divisions such as countries, states, boundaries and capitals. Thematic maps show one particular theme, such as rainfall, population density or road networks.

extraFaqs.q: Why do political maps change but physical maps rarely do?
extraFaqs.a: Political maps record boundaries agreed by governments, and those decisions change — India's map changed when Telangana was created in 2014. Physical maps record natural features such as mountains and rivers, which change only over geological timescales.

extraFaqs.q: What are the three components of a map?
extraFaqs.a: Distance (shown by the scale), direction (shown by a north line or compass rose) and symbols (standard signs and colours). All three must be present for a map to be read correctly.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a map and a globe?
extraFaqs.a: A globe is a true three-dimensional model of the Earth, so shapes and sizes stay accurate, but it cannot show small areas in detail and is awkward to carry. A map is flat, so some distortion is unavoidable, but it can show a small area in great detail and is easy to fold, print and compare.

evaporation-and-sublimation.ncertRef: NCERT Class 9 Science, Chapter 1 — Matter in Our Surroundings.

explainers.term: Evaporation: liquid to gas, from the surface only
paras: Evaporation is a liquid changing into vapour at temperatures below its boiling point. The key idea is that it happens only at the surface. Particles in a liquid move at a range of speeds; a few at the surface happen to be moving fast enough to escape the attraction of their neighbours and leave as vapour. This is why a puddle dries at 30 °C even though water boils at 100 °C.

Because the fastest particles are the ones that escape, the average energy of the particles left behind falls — and lower average energy means lower temperature. That is why evaporation causes cooling. It is why you feel cold stepping out of a swimming pool, why sweating cools you down, and why water stays cool in an earthen pot: water seeps through the pores, evaporates from the outside, and takes heat from the pot with it.

explainers.term: Sublimation: solid straight to gas
paras: Sublimation is a solid changing directly into vapour without ever becoming a liquid. The liquid state is skipped entirely, and that single fact is the whole difference. Camphor left in a cupboard shrinks and disappears without ever leaving a puddle; naphthalene balls behave the same way.

The standard laboratory demonstration uses ammonium chloride heated in an inverted funnel over a china dish: the solid turns straight to vapour, rises, and re-forms as a solid on the cool glass above. Iodine and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) also sublime — dry ice is named for exactly this reason, since it leaves no liquid behind.

sections.h: The four factors that speed up evaporation
paras: This list is examined directly almost every year. Learn all four with a reason for each.
bullets: Surface area — more exposed surface means more particles positioned to escape. Clothes spread out dry faster than clothes bundled up.
Temperature — heat gives particles more kinetic energy, so more of them can break free. Clothes dry faster in the sun.
Humidity — humidity is how much water vapour the air already holds. When the air is nearly saturated, evaporation slows. This is why clothes take so long to dry during the monsoon.
Wind speed — moving air carries away the vapour that has just formed, keeping the air above the liquid unsaturated so more can evaporate. Clothes dry faster on a breezy day.

sections.h: All six changes of state, and their names
paras: Naming the reverse processes correctly separates a full-mark answer from a partial one.
bullets: Melting (fusion) — solid to liquid, at the melting point.
Freezing (solidification) — liquid to solid, the reverse of melting.
Vaporisation — liquid to gas. This covers both evaporation (at the surface, any temperature) and boiling (throughout the liquid, at the boiling point only).
Condensation — gas to liquid, the reverse of vaporisation. Dew on grass, water droplets on a cold glass.
Sublimation — solid straight to gas.
Deposition (also called desublimation) — gas straight to solid, the reverse of sublimation. Frost forming on a cold window is water vapour depositing as ice.

sections.h: Why latent heat matters here
paras: During a change of state, heat is absorbed or released but the temperature does not change. That hidden heat is called latent heat, and it goes into overcoming the forces holding the particles together rather than into raising temperature.

The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg and the latent heat of vaporisation of water is 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg. The vaporisation figure is far larger because the particles must be separated completely, not merely loosened. This is why steam at 100 °C causes a much worse burn than water at 100 °C: the steam releases all that extra latent heat as it condenses on your skin.

examples.t: Wet clothes drying on a line
examples.d: Evaporation. Liquid water at the fabric's surface becomes vapour well below 100 °C.

examples.t: A camphor tablet vanishing over a week
examples.d: Sublimation. The solid became vapour directly — the shelf underneath stayed dry.

examples.t: Feeling cold after a swim
examples.d: Evaporation causes cooling. The fastest water particles leave your skin, taking energy with them.

examples.t: Dry ice producing white fog
examples.d: Sublimation. Solid carbon dioxide becomes gas directly; the visible fog is water vapour from the air condensing in the cold.

examples.t: Frost on a windowpane
examples.d: Deposition — the reverse of sublimation. Water vapour becomes solid ice without becoming liquid first.

mistakes: Saying sublimation is 'fast evaporation'. They start from different states entirely — sublimation starts from a solid, evaporation from a liquid.
Claiming evaporation only happens at the boiling point. It happens at all temperatures, because it only needs surface particles with enough energy.
Confusing evaporation with boiling. Evaporation is a surface phenomenon at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.
Forgetting that evaporation causes cooling, and forgetting to explain why (the higher-energy particles leave).
Naming the reverse of sublimation as 'condensation'. Gas to solid is deposition; condensation is gas to liquid.

quiz.q: Camphor left in the open disappears without leaving any liquid. This is:
quiz.why: The solid turned straight into vapour with no liquid stage — the definition of sublimation.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT increase the rate of evaporation?
quiz.why: Higher humidity means the air already holds a lot of water vapour, which slows evaporation down.

quiz.q: Water in an earthen pot stays cool because:
options: Water evaporates through the pores and takes heat with it
quiz.why: Water seeps through the porous clay and evaporates from the surface; the escaping high-energy particles carry heat away, cooling what remains.

quiz.q: The change of a gas directly into a solid is called:
quiz.why: Gas to solid is deposition (desublimation). Sublimation is the opposite direction, solid to gas.

extraFaqs.q: Why does evaporation cause cooling?
extraFaqs.a: Only the fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape as vapour. When they leave, the average energy of the particles remaining is lower — and lower average kinetic energy means a lower temperature. The energy needed to escape is drawn from the liquid and its surroundings.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
extraFaqs.a: Evaporation happens only at the surface of a liquid and at any temperature below boiling point. Boiling happens throughout the whole liquid, forming bubbles, and only at one fixed temperature — the boiling point (100 °C for water at normal pressure).

extraFaqs.q: Give three substances that sublime.
extraFaqs.a: Camphor, naphthalene (mothballs), ammonium chloride, iodine and solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) all sublime. Ammonium chloride is the one usually used in the school laboratory demonstration.

extraFaqs.q: Why does steam at 100 °C burn more badly than water at 100 °C?
extraFaqs.a: Steam carries an extra 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg of latent heat of vaporisation. When it touches skin it condenses and releases all of that energy on top of the heat from its temperature, so the burn is far more severe.

equator-and-prime-meridian.ncertRef: NCERT Class 6 Geography, Chapter 2 — Globe: Latitudes and Longitudes.

explainers.term: The Equator — the 0° line of latitude
paras: The Equator is an imaginary circle drawn around the Earth exactly midway between the North and South Poles. It is labelled 0° latitude, and it divides the globe into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

It is the longest of all the parallels of latitude, roughly 40,075 km around, because it sits at the widest part of the Earth. Every other parallel is shorter, shrinking to a single point at each pole. The Equator is a real physical reference: the Sun is overhead there twice a year, at the equinoxes, and countries on it have almost equal day and night all year round.

explainers.term: The Prime Meridian — the 0° line of longitude
paras: The Prime Meridian is the semicircle of longitude that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole through Greenwich, near London. It is labelled 0° longitude and divides the globe into the Eastern Hemisphere and the Western Hemisphere.

Unlike the Equator, its position is a human choice, not a natural one. There is nothing physically special about Greenwich; an international conference in 1884 simply agreed to put zero there, and the world's clocks have been set from it ever since. Any meridian could have been chosen — and before 1884, different countries used different ones.

sections.h: Parallels of latitude — the important ones
paras: There are 181 parallels in total: 90 north, 90 south, and the Equator itself. Five carry names, and CBSE expects all five with their values.
bullets: Equator — 0°, the reference line.
Tropic of Cancer — 23½° N. Passes through eight Indian states, which is a favourite exam question.
Tropic of Capricorn — 23½° S.
Arctic Circle — 66½° N.
Antarctic Circle — 66½° S.

These lines mark the heat zones: the Torrid Zone between the two Tropics (the Sun is overhead here at some point in the year), the two Temperate Zones between each Tropic and its Circle, and the two Frigid Zones beyond the Circles.

sections.h: Meridians of longitude and the link to time
paras: There are 360 meridians — 180 east and 180 west of the Prime Meridian. Unlike parallels, all meridians are the same length and all of them meet at the two poles, which is why they are semicircles rather than circles.
Longitude and time are directly connected. The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so it turns 15° in one hour and 1° in four minutes. Moving east, local time runs ahead; moving west, it falls behind.

India's Standard Meridian is 82°30′ E, passing through Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. Because 82.5 × 4 minutes = 330 minutes, Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time. The 180° meridian is the International Date Line, where the date changes by one day.

sections.h: The clean way to keep them straight
paras: Latitude lines run east-west but measure how far north or south you are. Longitude lines run north-south but measure how far east or west you are. Students reverse this constantly.

A memory hook that works: latitude sounds like 'ladder' — the rungs are horizontal and you climb them north or south. Longitude lines are 'long' — they run the long way, pole to pole. Together, a latitude and a longitude give a unique address for any point on Earth: Delhi is roughly 28.6° N, 77.2° E.

examples.t: A place at 0° latitude, 0° longitude
examples.d: The single point where the Equator meets the Prime Meridian, in the Gulf of Guinea off West Africa.

examples.t: Working out IST
examples.d: 82°30′ E × 4 minutes per degree = 330 minutes = 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

examples.t: Why Arunachal Pradesh sees sunrise before Gujarat
examples.d: Arunachal is further east. The Earth rotates west to east, so eastern longitudes meet the Sun first — about two hours earlier across India's width.

examples.t: The Tropic of Cancer in India
examples.d: 23½° N cuts across the middle of the country, passing through eight states including Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal and Mizoram.

mistakes: Calling the Prime Meridian a full circle. It is a semicircle from pole to pole; the Equator is the full circle.
Saying all parallels are equal in length. Only meridians are equal; parallels shrink towards the poles.
Writing that the Equator divides the Earth into east and west. It divides north and south — the Prime Meridian does east and west.
Forgetting that 1° of longitude equals 4 minutes of time, which is needed for every IST calculation.
Giving India's Standard Meridian as 82° E. It is 82°30′ E — the half degree is what makes IST 5:30 rather than 5:28.

quiz.q: The Equator divides the Earth into:
quiz.why: The Equator runs east-west at 0° latitude, separating the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. East and west are divided by the Prime Meridian.

quiz.q: India's Standard Meridian is:
quiz.why: 82°30′ E passes through Mirzapur; multiplying 82.5 by 4 minutes gives IST as GMT + 5:30.

quiz.q: How many parallels of latitude are there in total?
quiz.why: 90 in the Northern Hemisphere, 90 in the Southern, plus the Equator itself makes 181.

quiz.q: The Earth rotates through 1° of longitude in:
quiz.why: 360° in 24 hours is 15° per hour, so 1° takes 60 ÷ 15 = 4 minutes.

extraFaqs.q: Why was Greenwich chosen for the Prime Meridian?
extraFaqs.a: It was an international agreement, not a natural fact. At an 1884 conference the world agreed to place 0° longitude at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, largely because British nautical charts were already the most widely used. Any meridian could have been chosen instead.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between latitude and longitude?
extraFaqs.a: Latitude measures distance north or south of the Equator, and its lines run east-west as parallels of unequal length. Longitude measures distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, and its lines run north-south as semicircles of equal length that meet at the poles.

extraFaqs.q: What is the International Date Line?
extraFaqs.a: It is roughly the 180° meridian, on the opposite side of the globe from the Prime Meridian. Crossing it changes the calendar date by one day. It bends in places so that island groups and countries are not split across two different dates.

extraFaqs.q: Why is Indian Standard Time 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT?
extraFaqs.a: India's Standard Meridian is 82°30′ E. Since the Earth turns 1° every 4 minutes, 82.5° × 4 = 330 minutes, which is 5 hours 30 minutes. A single standard meridian is used so the whole country keeps one time.

square-and-cube.ncertRef: NCERT Class 8 Maths, Chapter 6 — Squares and Square Roots and Chapter 7 — Cubes and Cube Roots; shapes covered in Class 8 Chapter 10 — Visualising Solid Shapes.

explainers.term: This question has two different answers — check which one you need
paras: 'Difference between square and cube' is asked in two quite separate senses, and answering the wrong one loses full marks. The first sense is arithmetic: squaring a number versus cubing it. The second is geometric: the square as a flat 2D shape versus the cube as a 3D solid.

Both are on the CBSE syllabus and both are covered below. If the question mentions numbers, roots or exponents, it is the arithmetic sense. If it mentions faces, edges, vertices, area or volume, it is the shape sense.

explainers.term: Sense 1 — squaring versus cubing a number
paras: The square of a number is that number multiplied by itself once: n² = n × n. So 5² = 25. The cube is the number multiplied by itself twice more: n³ = n × n × n. So 5³ = 125.

The exponent is the only difference in the formula, but the growth rates diverge fast. For n = 10, the square is 100 and the cube is 1,000. For n = 20, the square is 400 and the cube is 8,000 — twenty times larger. This is why volume grows so much faster than area when an object is scaled up.

explainers.term: Sense 2 — the square shape versus the cube solid
paras: A square is a two-dimensional (flat) shape with four equal sides and four right angles. It has length and breadth but no thickness, so it has area but no volume.

A cube is a three-dimensional solid built from six identical square faces. It has length, breadth and height, so it has both surface area and volume. A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. In effect, a square is one face of a cube — the cube is what you get when a square is given depth.

sections.h: The formulas you need for both
paras: Learn these as pairs; questions very often ask for one of each.
bullets: Square of a number: n² = n × n. Square root: √n, the number which when squared gives n.
Cube of a number: n³ = n × n × n. Cube root: ∛n, the number which when cubed gives n.
Square shape, side a: Area = a², Perimeter = 4a, Diagonal = a√2.
Cube solid, edge a: Volume = a³, Total surface area = 6a², Lateral surface area = 4a², Space diagonal = a√3.

sections.h: Properties of square numbers that save time in exams
paras: These let you reject wrong options instantly in an MCQ, without calculating.
bullets: A perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8. If a number ends in one of those digits, it cannot be a perfect square.
A perfect square never has an odd number of zeros at the end. 100 is a perfect square; 1000 is not.
The square of an even number is even; the square of an odd number is odd.
Squares are never negative. Cubes can be — (−4)³ = −64, while (−4)² = +16. This sign behaviour is the most examined difference between the two operations.
The sum of the first n odd numbers equals n². For example 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4².

sections.h: Perfect squares and perfect cubes to memorise
paras: Notice that 1 and 64 appear in both lists — they are both perfect squares and perfect cubes (64 = 8² = 4³). The next such number is 729 = 27² = 9³.

examples.t: Square and cube of 7
examples.d: 7² = 49. 7³ = 343. The cube is seven times the square, which is always true: n³ = n² × n.

examples.t: A square tile of side 5 cm
examples.d: Area = 5² = 25 cm². Perimeter = 4 × 5 = 20 cm. There is no volume — the tile is treated as flat.

examples.t: A cubical box of edge 5 cm
examples.d: Volume = 5³ = 125 cm³. Total surface area = 6 × 5² = 150 cm². It has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

examples.t: Why sign matters
examples.d: (−3)² = 9, but (−3)³ = −27. Squaring destroys the negative sign; cubing keeps it.

mistakes: Answering only the number sense when the question meant the shapes, or vice versa. Read the question for the words 'faces', 'volume' or 'area'.
Writing the total surface area of a cube as 4a². That is the lateral surface area; the total is 6a² because a cube has six faces.
Assuming a cube is 'a square in 3D' and therefore has 4 faces. It has 6.
Thinking a cube of a negative number is positive. Only even powers force a positive result.
Mixing up a cube (all edges equal) with a cuboid (a box whose length, breadth and height can differ).

quiz.q: What is the cube of 6?
quiz.why: 6³ = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216. 36 is the square, and 1296 is 6⁴.

quiz.q: How many edges does a cube have?
quiz.why: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

quiz.q: Which of these cannot be a perfect square?
quiz.why: 128 ends in 8, and no perfect square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8.

quiz.q: The total surface area of a cube of edge 4 cm is:
quiz.why: Total surface area = 6a² = 6 × 16 = 96 cm². 64 cm³ would be its volume.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a square and a cube?
extraFaqs.a: In arithmetic, the square of a number multiplies it by itself once (n² = n × n) while the cube multiplies it by itself twice more (n³ = n × n × n). In geometry, a square is a flat 2D shape with four equal sides and only area, while a cube is a 3D solid made of six square faces with both surface area and volume.

extraFaqs.q: Is a cube made of squares?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. A cube is bounded by six identical square faces. That is why its total surface area is 6a² — six squares, each of area a².

extraFaqs.q: Can a number be both a perfect square and a perfect cube?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. Such numbers are perfect sixth powers. The first few are 1, 64 (which is 8² and 4³) and 729 (which is 27² and 9³).

extraFaqs.q: Why is the cube of a negative number negative?
extraFaqs.a: Cubing multiplies three negative factors together. Two negatives give a positive, and the third negative makes the result negative again. Squaring uses only two factors, so the negatives always cancel and the answer is positive.

transpiration-and-translocation.ncertRef: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 6 — Life Processes (transport in plants); introduced in Class 7, Chapter 11.

explainers.term: Transpiration — losing water on purpose
paras: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly the leaves. Most of it escapes through tiny pores called stomata, each guarded by a pair of bean-shaped guard cells that open the pore when they swell with water and close it when they lose water.

It sounds wasteful — a large tree can lose hundreds of litres a day — but the plant gains three things from it. It creates the suction that pulls water up from the roots, it cools the leaf in the way sweating cools you, and it carries dissolved minerals upward with the water stream.

explainers.term: Translocation — moving food where it is needed
paras: Translocation is the transport of the soluble products of photosynthesis — mainly sucrose, along with amino acids — from where they are made to where they are needed. It happens in the phloem, and unlike transpiration it costs the plant energy in the form of ATP.

The tissue that supplies the food is called the source, usually a green leaf. The part that receives it is the sink — a root, a growing shoot tip, a developing fruit or a storage organ. Because sinks exist above and below the leaves, translocation moves food both upward and downward, which is the detail students most often get wrong.

sections.h: Xylem versus phloem — the two transport tissues
paras: Almost every question on this topic reduces to knowing which tissue does what. Learn these as a contrasting pair.
bullets: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals. Phloem carries prepared food (sucrose).
Xylem moves material only upward, from root to leaf. Phloem moves food in both directions, source to sink.
Xylem is made of dead cells — tracheids and vessels with no living contents, which is why it forms hollow tubes. Phloem is made of living cells — sieve tubes and their companion cells.
Xylem transport is passive: no energy is spent, because transpiration pull does the work. Phloem transport is active and needs ATP.
Xylem elements are lignified for strength; phloem sieve tubes have perforated sieve plates that let material pass between cells.

sections.h: How transpiration pull actually lifts water
paras: As water evaporates from the leaf surface, it leaves the cells there slightly short of water. That creates a suction, and because water molecules stick to one another (cohesion) and to the xylem walls (adhesion), the whole column of water in the xylem is pulled upward as one continuous thread.

This suction force is called transpiration pull, and it is strong enough to raise water to the top of the tallest trees without the plant spending any energy. It is the reason transpiration is described as a necessary evil rather than simply a loss.

sections.h: What changes the rate of transpiration
paras: The factors mirror those for evaporation, because transpiration is evaporation happening through a leaf.
bullets: Temperature — higher temperature speeds it up.
Humidity — high humidity slows it down, since the surrounding air already holds water vapour.
Wind speed — moving air carries vapour away and speeds it up.
Light — stomata open in light and close in the dark, so transpiration is much higher during the day.
Available soil water — a plant short of water closes its stomata to conserve what it has.

examples.t: Water droplets inside a polythene bag tied over a leafy shoot
examples.d: Transpiration. Water vapour left the leaves and condensed on the cool plastic.

examples.t: Sugar reaching a developing mango
examples.d: Translocation. The fruit is a sink; sucrose made in the leaves travels to it through the phloem.

examples.t: A wilting plant at noon
examples.d: Transpiration is outpacing absorption, so the cells lose turgor. The plant closes its stomata to slow the loss.

examples.t: A potato tuber swelling underground
examples.d: Translocation moving food downward to a storage sink — proof that phloem transport is not one-directional.

mistakes: Saying translocation happens in the xylem. Food moves in the phloem; the xylem carries water and minerals.
Writing that translocation only moves food downwards. It moves to any sink, above or below the leaves.
Calling transpiration simply a waste of water. It generates the transpiration pull that lifts water and it cools the plant.
Forgetting that phloem transport needs energy while xylem transport does not.
Confusing guttation with transpiration — guttation is the loss of liquid water droplets from leaf margins, not water vapour.

quiz.q: Food prepared in the leaves is transported through the:
quiz.why: Phloem carries the soluble products of photosynthesis from source to sink. Xylem carries water and minerals.

quiz.q: Transpiration mainly takes place through:
quiz.why: Stomata are the pores on leaves through which most water vapour escapes.

quiz.q: Which statement about xylem is correct?
options: It is made of living cells
It is made of dead cells and moves water upward
quiz.why: Xylem consists of dead, lignified tracheids and vessels, and moves water upward passively using transpiration pull.

quiz.q: Translocation requires energy because:
options: It is an active process using ATP
quiz.why: Phloem loading and unloading are active processes that consume ATP, unlike passive xylem transport.

extraFaqs.q: Is transpiration a necessary evil?
extraFaqs.a: Yes, and that is the phrase textbooks use. The plant loses a great deal of water, which is the 'evil' part. But the loss generates the transpiration pull that raises water from the roots, cools the leaves, and carries dissolved minerals upward — so the plant cannot do without it.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between the source and the sink in translocation?
extraFaqs.a: The source is the part that makes or releases food, usually a photosynthesising leaf. The sink is any part that uses or stores it — roots, growing tips, flowers, fruits and storage organs. Food always moves from source to sink, which can be in any direction.

extraFaqs.q: Why does transpiration decrease in humid weather?
extraFaqs.a: The surrounding air already holds a lot of water vapour, so the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the air is small. With a weaker gradient, less water evaporates from the leaf surface.

extraFaqs.q: What is guttation and how is it different from transpiration?
extraFaqs.a: Guttation is the loss of liquid water as droplets from the margins of leaves, usually at night or early morning when humidity is high and root pressure is strong. Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour, mainly through stomata during the day.

saturated-vs-unsaturated-solution.ncertRef: NCERT Class 9 Science, Chapter 2 — Is Matter Around Us Pure?

explainers.term: Saturated solution — the point where no more will dissolve
paras: A saturated solution is one that has dissolved the maximum amount of solute it can hold at a particular temperature. Add any more and it simply settles at the bottom undissolved, however long you stir.

The phrase 'at a particular temperature' is not optional. A solution saturated at 20 °C is usually no longer saturated at 60 °C, because most solids dissolve more readily when hot. Leaving the temperature out of a definition is the single most common way students lose a mark here.

explainers.term: Unsaturated solution — there is still room
paras: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than the maximum it could hold at that temperature. Add a little more and it dissolves.

There is also a third, less familiar state. If a hot saturated solution is cooled very slowly and left undisturbed, it can end up holding more solute than it should be able to. This is a supersaturated solution, and it is unstable — a single crystal or even a jolt will make the excess solute crystallise out at once.

sections.h: Solubility, and how to state it properly
paras: Solubility is the amount of a solute that saturates 100 grams of solvent at a given temperature. It is the number that tells you where the saturation point sits.

So saying 'the solubility of potassium nitrate is 32 g at 20 °C' means 100 g of water at 20 °C will dissolve 32 g of potassium nitrate and no more. Different solutes have very different solubilities in the same solvent, and the same solute has different solubilities in different solvents.

sections.h: What temperature does — and the exception for gases
paras: For most solids, solubility increases as temperature rises. Heating a saturated sugar solution lets more sugar dissolve, which is exactly how sugar syrup is made.

Gases behave the opposite way: their solubility decreases as temperature rises. This is why a warm fizzy drink goes flat faster than a cold one, and why fish struggle in warm water — it holds less dissolved oxygen. Examiners like this reversal because it catches students who have memorised only the solid case.

sections.h: How to express concentration
paras: Concentration means how much solute is present in a given quantity of solution. Two formulas are on the syllabus.
bullets: Mass by mass percentage = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.
Mass by volume percentage = (mass of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100.
Note that mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent. Dividing by the mass of the solvent alone is a frequent slip.
A dilute solution has a small amount of solute; a concentrated solution has a large amount. These are relative terms, unlike saturated and unsaturated which have exact meanings.

examples.t: Sugar settling at the bottom of a cold glass of tea
examples.d: The solution is saturated at that temperature — no more sugar can dissolve until it is heated.

examples.t: Two spoons of salt dissolving completely in a litre of water
examples.d: Unsaturated. The solution can still take more salt.

examples.t: A hot saturated salt solution cooling and forming crystals
examples.d: Solubility falls as the solution cools, so the excess solute can no longer stay dissolved and crystallises out.

examples.t: A warm cold drink going flat quickly
examples.d: Gas solubility decreases with temperature, so dissolved carbon dioxide escapes faster.

mistakes: Defining a saturated solution without mentioning temperature. The definition is meaningless without it.
Treating 'saturated' and 'concentrated' as the same thing. Concentrated just means a lot of solute; saturated means the exact maximum has been reached.
Assuming solubility always rises with temperature. It does for most solids, but falls for gases.
Calculating mass percentage using the mass of the solvent instead of the mass of the whole solution.
Forgetting that a supersaturated solution exists and is unstable.

quiz.q: A solution that can dissolve no more solute at a given temperature is:
quiz.why: Saturated means the maximum amount of solute for that temperature has already dissolved.

quiz.q: The solubility of most solids in water when temperature increases:
quiz.why: Most solids dissolve more readily in hot solvent. Gases are the exception — their solubility falls as temperature rises.

quiz.q: If 20 g of salt is dissolved in 80 g of water, the mass by mass percentage is:
quiz.why: Mass of solution = 20 + 80 = 100 g. So (20 ÷ 100) × 100 = 20%. Dividing by 80 instead of 100 gives the wrong 25%.

quiz.q: A warm fizzy drink goes flat faster because:
quiz.why: Unlike solids, gases become less soluble as temperature rises, so dissolved carbon dioxide escapes more quickly.

extraFaqs.q: What is a supersaturated solution?
extraFaqs.a: It is a solution holding more dissolved solute than its saturation point allows at that temperature. It is made by cooling a hot saturated solution slowly without disturbing it, and it is unstable — adding a seed crystal or shaking it makes the excess solute crystallise out immediately.

extraFaqs.q: Is a saturated solution always concentrated?
extraFaqs.a: No. Saturated means the maximum possible amount has dissolved for that solute and temperature, which for a poorly soluble substance may be a very small amount. A saturated solution of a barely soluble salt is saturated but still dilute.

extraFaqs.q: How do you turn a saturated solution into an unsaturated one?
extraFaqs.a: Heat it, if the solute is a solid — higher temperature raises solubility, so the same amount of dissolved solute is no longer the maximum. Alternatively, add more solvent.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between solubility and concentration?
extraFaqs.a: Solubility is a fixed property: the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a stated temperature. Concentration is how much solute a particular solution actually contains, which can be anything from nearly zero up to the solubility limit.

balanced-and-unbalanced-force.ncertRef: NCERT Class 9 Science, Chapter 9 — Force and Laws of Motion.

explainers.term: Balanced forces — everything cancels
paras: Forces acting on an object are balanced when they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the net (resultant) force is zero. The object's state of motion does not change: if it was at rest it stays at rest, and if it was moving at constant velocity it keeps moving at that same velocity in the same direction.

Balanced forces cannot make an object accelerate, but they can still do something — they can change its shape. Squeezing a rubber ball equally from both sides does not move it, yet the ball deforms. That is a favourite one-mark question.

explainers.term: Unbalanced forces — something is left over
paras: Forces are unbalanced when they do not cancel, so the net force is not zero. An unbalanced force always produces acceleration: the object starts moving, speeds up, slows down or changes direction.

The crucial point students miss is that acceleration means any change in velocity, not just speeding up. A car braking is accelerating (negatively), and a car going round a bend at constant speed is accelerating too, because its direction is changing. Both need an unbalanced force.

sections.h: Newton's three laws, and where each one fits
paras: This topic is really an introduction to the laws of motion, so the laws are what the questions test.
bullets: First law (law of inertia) — an object stays at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced force. This law defines what force does; balanced forces are exactly the case where nothing changes.

Second law — the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied unbalanced force and takes place in its direction. It gives the equation F = ma, which lets you calculate how much acceleration a given unbalanced force produces.

Third law — to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Note carefully that these two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other out. Confusing a third-law pair with balanced forces is the classic error in this chapter.

sections.h: Inertia, and why mass is the measure of it
paras: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. The greater an object's mass, the greater its inertia — which is why mass is called the quantitative measure of inertia.

This is why a loaded truck is harder to start moving and harder to stop than an empty one, and why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly: their bodies tend to keep moving even though the bus has slowed.

sections.h: Friction: the force that hides in every question
paras: A ball rolled across the ground eventually stops. Students often conclude that motion needs a continuous force, which is exactly backwards. The ball stops because friction acts on it as an unbalanced force opposing its motion.

Remove the friction and the ball would keep rolling forever, as Newton's first law says. Whenever a question asks why a moving object slows down on its own, friction (or air resistance) is the unbalanced force to name.

examples.t: A book resting on a table
examples.d: Its weight acts downward and the table's normal reaction acts upward, equal and opposite. Balanced forces — the book stays at rest.

examples.t: A tug of war with neither side moving
examples.d: Both teams pull equally hard in opposite directions. The net force is zero, so the rope does not accelerate.

examples.t: The moment one tug-of-war team pulls harder
examples.d: The forces become unbalanced. There is now a net force, and the rope accelerates towards the stronger team.

examples.t: A car turning a corner at steady speed
examples.d: Unbalanced force. The speed is constant but the direction is changing, so the car is accelerating and a net force must be acting.

mistakes: Thinking balanced forces mean the object must be stationary. An object moving at constant velocity also has balanced forces on it.
Believing a moving object needs a continuous force to keep moving. It only appears that way because friction is constantly opposing it.
Treating an action-reaction pair as balanced forces. They act on two different bodies, so they never cancel out.
Assuming acceleration only means speeding up. Slowing down and changing direction are also acceleration.
Forgetting that balanced forces can still change an object's shape.

quiz.q: An object moving at constant velocity in a straight line has:
options: An unbalanced force acting on it
quiz.why: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so the net force is zero — the forces are balanced. Forces may still be acting; they simply cancel.

quiz.q: A ball rolling on the ground slows down and stops because of:
options: Friction acting as an unbalanced force
quiz.why: Friction opposes the motion and is unbalanced, producing a negative acceleration until the ball stops.

quiz.q: Which is the correct measure of inertia?
quiz.why: The greater the mass, the greater the resistance to a change in the state of motion, so mass is the quantitative measure of inertia.

quiz.q: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg body. Its acceleration is:
quiz.why: From F = ma, a = F ÷ m = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s².

extraFaqs.q: Can balanced forces change the shape of an object?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. Balanced forces cannot change an object's state of motion, but they can deform it. Pressing a rubber ball equally from both sides leaves it stationary while clearly changing its shape.

extraFaqs.q: Why do passengers fall forward when a bus stops suddenly?
extraFaqs.a: Because of inertia of motion. The bus is stopped by an unbalanced braking force, but the passengers' bodies tend to continue moving forward at the original speed until a force acts on them.

extraFaqs.q: Are action and reaction forces balanced forces?
extraFaqs.a: No, and this is the most common confusion in the chapter. Action and reaction are equal and opposite but act on two different bodies. Balanced forces act on the same body, which is why they cancel and produce no acceleration.

extraFaqs.q: Does zero net force mean zero velocity?
extraFaqs.a: No. Zero net force means zero acceleration — the velocity does not change. That velocity can be zero (at rest) or any constant value (uniform motion in a straight line).

explainers.term: What a map is
paras: A map is a drawing of the Earth's surface, or a part of it, on a flat sheet according to a scale. It can cover anything from a district to the whole world, and because it must fit a large area onto a small sheet, it shows features in a generalised way using symbols rather than in full detail.
Every map is drawn to a scale, which is the ratio between the distance on the paper and the actual distance on the ground. Without a scale a drawing is not a map — it is a sketch.

explainers.term: What a plan is
paras: A plan is a drawing of a very small area — a room, a house, a school building, a plot of land — drawn to a large scale. Because so little ground is being represented, a plan can show fine detail that no map could: the thickness of a wall, the position of a door, the exact dimensions of a room.
This is why an architect works with plans, not maps. If you need to know the length and breadth of a classroom, a map of your city is useless; a plan of the school building answers it immediately.

sections.h: The third kind of drawing: a sketch
paras: NCERT names three drawings, and students who list only two lose marks. A sketch is a rough drawing based on memory and a rough observation, and it is NOT drawn to scale.
So the full set is: a sketch (no scale, rough), a plan (large scale, very small area, high detail) and a map (smaller scale, large area, generalised). Scale is what separates all three.

sections.h: Large scale and small scale — the wording that trips everyone up
paras: A large-scale map shows a small area with a lot of detail. A small-scale map shows a large area with little detail. Almost every student reads this backwards on first meeting it.

The logic becomes clear from the fraction. A scale of 1:1,000 is a larger fraction than 1:1,000,000, so 1:1,000 is the larger scale — and at that scale a single sheet can only cover a small patch of ground, but it can show it in great detail. A plan uses a large scale; a world map uses a very small scale.

sections.h: The three components every map must have
paras: These apply to plans as well and are examined directly.
bullets: Distance — expressed by the scale, so real distances can be worked out from the drawing.
Direction — usually a north arrow. The four cardinal directions are north, south, east and west; the intermediate ones are north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west.
Symbols — internationally agreed signs and colours for railways, roads, bridges, trees and buildings, so a map can be read regardless of the reader's language.

examples.t: Finding the width of your classroom
examples.d: Use a plan. Only a large-scale drawing of a small area carries that level of detail.

examples.t: Finding the route from Delhi to Jaipur
examples.d: Use a map. The area is far too large for a plan.

examples.t: A rough drawing of the way to a friend's house
examples.d: A sketch. It is drawn from memory and not to scale.

examples.t: An architect's drawing of a house
examples.d: A plan — every wall and door drawn to an exact large scale.

mistakes: Saying a plan is just a small map. A plan covers a very small area at a large scale with far more detail.
Forgetting that a sketch is the third category and is not drawn to scale.
Reversing large scale and small scale. Large scale = small area, more detail.
Writing that a plan does not need a scale. A plan is always drawn to scale — that is precisely what separates it from a sketch.
Leaving out the north direction, which is one of the three compulsory components.

quiz.q: A drawing of a very small area on a large scale is called a:
quiz.why: A plan shows a very small area, such as a room or a building, at a large scale with fine detail.

quiz.q: Which drawing is NOT made to scale?
quiz.why: A sketch is a rough drawing based on memory and observation, without a scale.

quiz.q: A large-scale map shows:
options: A large area with little detail
A small area with a lot of detail
quiz.why: Large scale means a bigger representative fraction, so less ground fits on the sheet and more detail can be shown.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three components of a map?
quiz.why: The three components are distance (scale), direction and symbols. Colour is part of the symbol system, not a separate component.

extraFaqs.q: What is the main difference between a map and a plan?
extraFaqs.a: A map shows a large area — a district, a country, the world — on a smaller scale, so features are generalised. A plan shows a very small area such as a room or a building on a large scale, so it can carry precise detail like wall thickness and room dimensions.

extraFaqs.q: Why can't a map show the details a plan shows?
extraFaqs.a: Because of scale. A map must fit a very large area onto a small sheet, so a whole building might occupy less than a millimetre. There is simply no room to draw individual walls or doors, so features are represented by symbols instead.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a sketch and a plan?
extraFaqs.a: A sketch is a rough drawing made from memory and not drawn to any scale, so distances on it mean nothing. A plan is drawn accurately to a large scale, so every measurement on it corresponds to a real measurement on the ground.

extraFaqs.q: Is a globe better than a map?
extraFaqs.a: Each is better for a different job. A globe is a true model of the Earth, so shapes, sizes and distances stay accurate, but it cannot show a small area in detail and is hard to carry. A map is flat so some distortion is unavoidable, but it can show a small area in great detail and is easy to print and carry.

prism-and-pyramid.ncertRef: NCERT Class 8 Maths, Chapter 10 — Visualising Solid Shapes; surface areas and volumes in Class 9 and Class 10.

explainers.term: A prism has two identical bases
paras: A prism is a solid with two identical, parallel polygonal faces called bases, joined by flat side faces that are always rectangles (or parallelograms). Slice a prism anywhere parallel to its base and you get exactly the same shape every time — the cross-section is uniform along its whole length.

Prisms are named after the shape of the base. A triangular prism has two triangular bases, a pentagonal prism has two pentagonal ones. A cuboid is a rectangular prism, and a cube is a square prism, which surprises most students the first time they meet it.

explainers.term: A pyramid has one base and a point
paras: A pyramid has just one polygonal base, and its side faces are triangles that all meet at a single point called the apex. The cross-section is not uniform: slice a pyramid parallel to its base and the slices get smaller and smaller as you approach the apex.

Pyramids are also named after the base. A triangular pyramid — also called a tetrahedron — has a triangular base and three triangular sides. A square pyramid, like the pyramids at Giza, has a square base and four triangular sides.

sections.h: Faces, edges and vertices — the numbers to know
paras: For a base with n sides, both solids follow a simple rule. Learning the rule beats memorising individual cases.
bullets: Prism with an n-sided base: n + 2 faces, 3n edges, 2n vertices. A triangular prism therefore has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.
Pyramid with an n-sided base: n + 1 faces, 2n edges, n + 1 vertices. A square pyramid therefore has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.
Both satisfy Euler's formula, F + V − E = 2. Check the triangular prism: 5 + 6 − 9 = 2. Check the square pyramid: 5 + 5 − 8 = 2.
Euler's formula is a fast way to verify an answer in the exam — if your three numbers do not give 2, one of them is wrong.

sections.h: The volume formulas, and the one-third that matters
paras: Volume of a prism = base area × height. Volume of a pyramid = ⅓ × base area × height.

That factor of one-third is the most examined single fact in this topic. It means a pyramid holds exactly one third of the prism that shares its base and height — three identical pyramids can be fitted together to fill their corresponding prism exactly.

The lateral surface of a prism is made of rectangles, so lateral surface area = perimeter of base × height. The lateral surface of a pyramid is made of triangles, so lateral surface area = ½ × perimeter of base × slant height. Note that a pyramid's formula uses the slant height, not the vertical height — mixing the two is a guaranteed lost mark.

sections.h: Telling them apart in one glance
paras: Count the bases. Two identical parallel bases means a prism; one base and an apex means a pyramid.
Or look at the side faces. Rectangles all round means a prism; triangles meeting at a point means a pyramid. Either test works instantly on a diagram.

examples.t: A Toblerone-style chocolate box
examples.d: A triangular prism — two identical triangular ends joined by three rectangles.

examples.t: The Great Pyramid of Giza
examples.d: A square pyramid — one square base and four triangular faces meeting at an apex.

examples.t: A brick
examples.d: A rectangular prism (a cuboid). Its cross-section is the same all the way along.

examples.t: Volume comparison
examples.d: A prism and a pyramid both with base area 12 cm² and height 5 cm: the prism holds 12 × 5 = 60 cm³, the pyramid ⅓ × 12 × 5 = 20 cm³, exactly one third.

mistakes: Forgetting the ⅓ in the volume of a pyramid. This is the most frequently lost mark in the topic.
Using the vertical height instead of the slant height when finding a pyramid's lateral surface area.
Not realising that a cube and a cuboid are prisms.
Counting a square pyramid as having 4 faces. It has 5 — four triangles plus the base.
Assuming the side faces of a prism must be squares. They are rectangles, and only in special cases squares.

quiz.q: How many faces does a square pyramid have?
quiz.why: Four triangular side faces plus the square base makes 5. The formula n + 1 gives 4 + 1 = 5.

quiz.q: The volume of a pyramid is what fraction of a prism with the same base and height?
quiz.why: Volume of a pyramid = ⅓ × base area × height, so it is exactly one third of the corresponding prism.

quiz.q: A triangular prism has how many edges?
quiz.why: For an n-sided base a prism has 3n edges, so 3 × 3 = 9. Check with Euler: 5 + 6 − 9 = 2.

quiz.q: Which solid has two identical parallel bases?
quiz.why: A prism is defined by two identical, parallel polygonal bases joined by rectangular side faces.

extraFaqs.q: Is a cube a prism or a pyramid?
extraFaqs.a: A cube is a prism — specifically a square prism. It has two identical parallel square bases joined by rectangular (in this case square) side faces, and its cross-section is the same all the way along.

extraFaqs.q: What is Euler's formula and how do I use it?
extraFaqs.a: Euler's formula states that F + V − E = 2, where F is the number of faces, V the vertices and E the edges of any convex polyhedron. Use it to check your answer: a square pyramid gives 5 + 5 − 8 = 2, so the counts are right.

extraFaqs.q: Why is a pyramid's volume one third of a prism's?
extraFaqs.a: Because three identical pyramids with the same base and height can be fitted together to fill the corresponding prism exactly. That geometric fact is where the ⅓ in the formula comes from.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between the height and the slant height of a pyramid?
extraFaqs.a: The height is the perpendicular distance from the apex straight down to the centre of the base. The slant height is the distance from the apex down the middle of a triangular side face to the base edge. Volume uses the height; lateral surface area uses the slant height.

conductor-and-semiconductor.ncertRef: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 11 — Electricity; band theory and doping in Class 12 Physics, Chapter 14 — Semiconductor Electronics.

explainers.term: Conductors — electrons are already free
paras: A conductor is a material through which electric current flows easily, because it contains a very large number of free electrons that are not bound to any one atom. Apply even a small voltage and those electrons drift, producing a current.

Conductors have very low resistivity, of the order of 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ ohm-metre. Silver is the best conductor, but copper and aluminium are used in practice because they are far cheaper. Their resistance increases as temperature rises: the atoms vibrate more vigorously, the drifting electrons collide with them more often, and the flow is impeded.

explainers.term: Semiconductors — conductivity you can control
paras: A semiconductor has a conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator, with resistivity roughly 10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ ohm-metre. Silicon and germanium are the standard examples, both from group 14 with four valence electrons.

Their defining behaviour is the opposite of a conductor's: the resistance of a semiconductor decreases as temperature rises. Heat frees more electrons from their covalent bonds, so more charge carriers become available. This is described as a negative temperature coefficient of resistance, and it is the single most examined contrast in the topic.

sections.h: Band theory — the reason for the difference
paras: Energy-band structure explains in one picture why these materials behave so differently.
bullets: In a conductor the valence band and the conduction band overlap, or the conduction band is partly filled. Electrons need almost no extra energy to move, so current flows freely.

In a semiconductor there is a small forbidden energy gap between the bands — about 1.1 eV for silicon and 0.7 eV for germanium. At absolute zero a pure semiconductor behaves as an insulator; at room temperature some electrons gain enough thermal energy to jump the gap.
In an insulator the forbidden gap is large, typically more than 3 eV, so under ordinary conditions almost no electrons can cross it and virtually no current flows.

When an electron leaves the valence band it leaves behind a vacancy called a hole, which behaves as a positive charge carrier. Semiconductors therefore conduct by both electrons and holes; conductors conduct by electrons alone.

sections.h: Doping — why semiconductors are so useful
paras: A pure (intrinsic) semiconductor is not very useful on its own. Adding a tiny, controlled amount of impurity — a process called doping — raises its conductivity enormously and lets engineers decide which kind of charge carrier dominates. The doped material is called an extrinsic semiconductor.

Adding a pentavalent impurity (five valence electrons: phosphorus, arsenic or antimony) leaves one spare electron per atom. Electrons become the majority carriers, and the result is an n-type semiconductor.

Adding a trivalent impurity (three valence electrons: boron, aluminium or gallium) leaves one bond short, creating a hole. Holes become the majority carriers, and the result is a p-type semiconductor. Joining a p-type and an n-type piece makes a p-n junction — the diode, and the foundation of every transistor, integrated circuit and solar cell.

sections.h: Where each is used
paras: Conductors are used wherever current simply has to be carried: copper wiring in homes, aluminium in overhead transmission lines, and the metal filaments and contacts inside appliances.

Semiconductors are used wherever current has to be controlled rather than merely carried: diodes, transistors, LEDs, integrated circuits, solar cells and thermistors. This is the practical difference — conductors transport electricity, semiconductors switch and amplify it.

examples.t: Copper household wiring
examples.d: A conductor. It has abundant free electrons and very low resistivity, so it carries current with little loss.

examples.t: A silicon chip in a phone
examples.d: A semiconductor. Its conductivity is controlled by doping, allowing millions of switches on one wafer.

examples.t: A wire getting hotter and its resistance rising
examples.d: Conductor behaviour — a positive temperature coefficient.

examples.t: A thermistor whose resistance falls when heated
examples.d: Semiconductor behaviour — a negative temperature coefficient, which is what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.

mistakes: Saying the resistance of a semiconductor increases with temperature. It decreases — this is the opposite of a conductor.
Describing a semiconductor as simply 'a weak conductor'. Its usefulness comes from being controllable by doping, not from its raw conductivity.
Forgetting that semiconductors conduct by holes as well as electrons.
Thinking doping makes the semiconductor electrically charged. The material stays neutral overall; doping only changes which carrier is in the majority.
Mixing up n-type and p-type. Pentavalent impurity gives n-type (extra electrons); trivalent gives p-type (holes).

quiz.q: When temperature increases, the resistance of a semiconductor:
quiz.why: Heat frees more electrons across the small forbidden gap, creating more charge carriers, so resistance falls. Conductors behave the opposite way.

quiz.q: Doping silicon with phosphorus produces:
quiz.why: Phosphorus is pentavalent, so it contributes a spare electron. Electrons become the majority carriers, giving n-type.

quiz.q: The forbidden energy gap in silicon is approximately:
quiz.why: Silicon's band gap is about 1.1 eV and germanium's about 0.7 eV. Insulators have gaps above roughly 3 eV.

quiz.q: In a conductor, the valence and conduction bands:
options: Are separated by a large gap
quiz.why: Overlapping or partly filled bands mean electrons need almost no extra energy to move, which is why conductors conduct freely.

extraFaqs.q: Why does a semiconductor's resistance fall when heated but a conductor's rise?
extraFaqs.a: In a conductor the number of free electrons is already fixed and very large; heating only makes the atoms vibrate more, so electrons collide more often and resistance rises. In a semiconductor heating actually creates new charge carriers by freeing electrons across the small band gap, and that increase outweighs the extra collisions, so resistance falls.

extraFaqs.q: What is a hole in a semiconductor?
extraFaqs.a: When an electron leaves its place in a covalent bond, it leaves a vacancy that behaves like a positive charge carrier. This vacancy is called a hole. Neighbouring electrons move into it, so the hole appears to move in the opposite direction to the electrons, contributing to the current.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors?
extraFaqs.a: An intrinsic semiconductor is pure, with equal numbers of electrons and holes and low conductivity. An extrinsic semiconductor has been deliberately doped with a small impurity, which greatly increases its conductivity and makes either electrons (n-type) or holes (p-type) the majority carriers.

extraFaqs.q: Why is silicon preferred over germanium?
extraFaqs.a: Silicon has a larger band gap (1.1 eV against 0.7 eV), so it is much less affected by heat and works reliably at higher temperatures. It is also far more abundant, cheaper, and forms a stable oxide layer that is essential for manufacturing integrated circuits.

explainers.term: Speed at an instant
paras: Speed is the distance travelled by an object in unit time: speed = distance ÷ time. It is a scalar quantity, meaning it has magnitude but no direction, and its SI unit is metre per second (m/s). Kilometre per hour is also common, and the conversion is 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s.
When people say 'the car was doing 60', they mean instantaneous speed — the speed at that particular moment, which is what a speedometer shows. It can change from second to second.

explainers.term: Average speed over a journey
paras: Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken. It is a single number that summarises a whole journey, however irregular that journey was.

The definition is the important bit: total distance over total time. It is NOT the average of the individual speeds. A car that covers half a journey at 40 km/h and the other half at 60 km/h does not average 50 km/h — it averages 48 km/h, because it spends more time at the slower speed. This trap appears in exams constantly.

sections.h: Uniform and non-uniform motion
paras: An object is in uniform motion when it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, however small those intervals. In that special case, the instantaneous speed and the average speed are the same number.

In non-uniform motion the object covers unequal distances in equal intervals — which describes almost all real motion, such as a bus in traffic. Here the instantaneous speed keeps changing, and the average speed is the only single figure that describes the whole journey.

sections.h: Speed versus velocity, and average velocity
paras: Speed is a scalar and uses distance, which is the total path length covered. Velocity is a vector and uses displacement, which is the shortest straight-line distance from start to finish, with direction.

So average speed = total distance ÷ total time, but average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time. For an object that returns to its starting point, the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero — even though the average speed is clearly not. A runner completing one lap of a track is the standard example.
Average velocity can also be found as (initial velocity + final velocity) ÷ 2, but only when the acceleration is uniform. Applying that shortcut to non-uniform motion is a common error.

sections.h: The two-part journey formula
paras: For a journey covered in two equal distances at speeds a and b, the average speed is 2ab ÷ (a + b) — the harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean. For 40 and 60 that gives (2 × 40 × 60) ÷ 100 = 48 km/h.

But if the two speeds are maintained for equal times rather than equal distances, the average genuinely is (a + b) ÷ 2 = 50 km/h. Read the question carefully to see whether it is equal distances or equal times — the two give different answers, and examiners know it.

examples.t: A car covering 120 km in 3 hours
examples.d: Average speed = 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h, regardless of how much it sped up or slowed down along the way.

examples.t: A runner completing one full lap of a 400 m track in 50 s
examples.d: Average speed = 400 ÷ 50 = 8 m/s. Average velocity = 0, because the displacement is zero — she finished where she started.

examples.t: Half a trip at 40 km/h, half at 60 km/h
examples.d: Average speed = 2(40)(60) ÷ 100 = 48 km/h, not 50, because more time is spent on the slower half.

examples.t: A speedometer reading 55 km/h
examples.d: Instantaneous speed — the speed at that exact moment, not the average for the journey.

mistakes: Averaging the two speeds directly when the distances are equal. Use 2ab ÷ (a + b) instead.
Using displacement in an average-speed calculation. Average speed uses total distance travelled.
Saying average velocity and average speed are always equal in magnitude. They are equal only when the motion is in a straight line without reversing.
Applying average velocity = (u + v) ÷ 2 to non-uniform acceleration. It holds only for uniform acceleration.
Forgetting the unit conversion: 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s, not 18/5.

quiz.q: A body covers 100 m in 20 s and the next 100 m in 30 s. Its average speed is:
quiz.why: Total distance 200 m, total time 50 s, so 200 ÷ 50 = 4 m/s. Averaging 5 and 3.33 would wrongly give 4.17.

quiz.q: A runner completes exactly one lap of a circular track. Her average velocity is:
quiz.why: She ends where she began, so her displacement is zero and average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 0.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a vector?
quiz.why: Velocity has both magnitude and direction. Speed, distance and time are scalars.

quiz.q: 72 km/h expressed in m/s is:
quiz.why: Multiply by 5/18: 72 × 5 ÷ 18 = 20 m/s.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between speed and average speed?
extraFaqs.a: Speed usually means the instantaneous speed — how fast an object is moving at one particular moment, which is what a speedometer shows. Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the whole journey, and it smooths out all the variations along the way.

extraFaqs.q: Can average speed be zero?
extraFaqs.a: Only if the object never moves at all. Average speed uses total distance, which can never be negative and is zero only if no distance was covered. Average velocity, by contrast, is zero whenever an object returns to its starting point.

extraFaqs.q: Why is the average of 40 km/h and 60 km/h not 50 km/h?
extraFaqs.a: Because over equal distances the object spends more time travelling at the slower speed, so the slower speed carries more weight. The correct formula for equal distances is 2ab ÷ (a + b), which gives 48 km/h. If the two speeds were held for equal times instead, the answer would genuinely be 50 km/h.

extraFaqs.q: Can an object have constant speed but changing velocity?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has constant speed, but its direction changes continuously, so its velocity is changing. That is why circular motion at constant speed still involves acceleration.

explainers.term: Speed — how fast
paras: Speed tells you how much distance an object covers in unit time: speed = distance ÷ time. Its SI unit is metre per second (m/s), and it is a scalar, so it has size but no direction.
Speed answers the question 'how fast is it going right now?' A number on its own is enough — 20 m/s is a complete statement of speed.

explainers.term: Acceleration — how quickly the velocity changes
paras: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v − u) ÷ t, where u is the initial velocity and v the final velocity. Its SI unit is metre per second squared (m/s²), and it is a vector, so direction matters.

Acceleration answers a different question: 'how quickly is the motion changing?' An object can have a huge speed and zero acceleration — a train cruising steadily at 100 km/h — or zero speed and a large acceleration, like a ball at the exact top of its flight, momentarily still but still accelerating downward at 9.8 m/s².

sections.h: The three equations of motion
paras: These apply only to uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line. Almost every numerical in the chapter uses one of them.
bullets: v = u + at — relates velocity and time.
s = ut + ½at² — relates distance and time.
v² = u² + 2as — relates velocity and distance, with no time term. Use this one when time is not given and not asked for.
Here u is initial velocity, v final velocity, a acceleration, t time and s distance travelled.
For a body falling freely, replace a with g = 9.8 m/s² (often taken as 10 m/s² for quick working). For a body thrown upward, g is negative because it opposes the motion.

sections.h: Positive, negative and zero acceleration
paras: Acceleration is positive when velocity increases in the direction of motion — the object speeds up. It is negative when velocity decreases; this is called retardation or deceleration, and braking is the everyday case.

Acceleration is zero when velocity does not change at all, which means the object is at rest or moving with uniform velocity in a straight line. Zero acceleration does not mean zero speed, and that distinction is worth marks.

sections.h: Reading motion graphs
